POST

> If you are in your forties or fifties and you have been reading about andropause, here is the part that nobody selling you something will lead with. There is nothing to buy for it.
>
> Andropause, often called the male menopause, is a popular name for the cluster of symptoms some men notice as testosterone gradually declines with age. The decline is real. But the NHS points out the term itself can be misleading, because unlike the menopause there is no single switch-off moment, and a lot of what gets blamed on it has other causes.
>
> That is why the first honest move is not a product. It is finding out where your testosterone actually sits, because a good share of the men reading about this do not have a testosterone problem at all, and money aimed at the wrong cause is money and hope down the drain.
>
> The second move is the unglamorous one, and it does real work here. Losing excess weight, lifting weights, sleeping properly, and easing off alcohol all move how men in this bracket feel. None of it is instant and none of it is glamorous, which is exactly why it gets skipped for something with a label on it.
>
> And some of this does not belong in a wellness test at all. It belongs with your doctor first.
>
> Erectile problems go to your GP rather than to a hormone panel. Erectile difficulty can be an early warning sign of narrowed arteries, because the blood vessels involved are small and show strain first, so it can flag heart risk well before anything else does (British Heart Foundation). If your mood is low, or you have lost interest in things you used to enjoy, please talk to your GP. That is a mental health conversation and it deserves one. Same if this is getting in the way of your daily life or your relationship, and same if you are under 40 with these symptoms, because age-related decline is a less likely explanation that early.
>
> What we do is narrow. We test, we explain the number, and we tell you the next step, including when that next step is your GP. We do not diagnose and we do not prescribe. And a low result is a reason to see your GP, not a reason to buy anything from us.
>
> The full version, including what else these symptoms usually turn out to be and why the time of day your blood is taken matters, is here: andro-prime.com/blog/andropause-male-menopause?utm_source=facebook

## Craft notes

- **Archetype:** Teacher, which `written-post-playbook.md` names as a Facebook default alongside Breakdown and Investigator. The older, more patient, more clinical-curious reader is the one this format exists for, and the post is built to stand on its own value without the link.
- **The de-sell is the post, not a disclaimer inside it.** `avatar-mark.md` §C records that the mainstream reader's anger about upsell is billing distrust ("had to pay for another one to confirm the results. There is no mention of this anywhere"), so the strongest thing we can say to him is where our own product stops. The low-result paragraph is the point of the post rather than a caveat at the end of it, and it should not be trimmed for length. **Note that the argument survived the loss of the number**, which is the useful thing to know about it: the de-sell was never carried by the threshold, it was carried by naming where we stop.
- **Device 7, understatement at the peak:** "There is nothing to buy for it." Six words, first paragraph, and the whole argument.
- **Structure chosen on avatar fit, not on ease of clearance.** The competing Facebook angle was "do all men go through it, and at what age", which is the article's cleanest standalone section and asks nothing awkward of compliance. It was rejected because its implicit ask is "revise your mental model of ageing", which gives this reader nothing to do on a Tuesday. The GP-trigger angle hands him four specific decisions, one of which may matter more than anything else on our site.
- **Native upload, and the link stays in the post body.** Facebook demotes engagement bait and this format takes a soft in-post router link rather than a first comment, per the playbook. One link, no link-dumping.
- **Nothing in the machine is close to this.** No existing asset names the GP-referral triggers, and none of them says out loud that a result below a threshold is a reason not to buy from us. `the-stack` is the nearest relative (a founder saying do not test yet), but that is a video, its subject is the lifestyle stack, and its de-sell is about timing rather than about which symptoms belong with a doctor. Do not schedule the two in the same week.

## Rails held

Written as an allowlist of what the copy does, never a list of what it avoids.

The post stays on the education side of the line throughout. It states what a popular label covers, quotes the NHS position on the term, names four situations that route to a doctor rather than to a test, and states the boundary of what this business does in the wording CA-028 §4 already approved. It names no ingredient, so the EFSA tables are not in play. It names no other provider and makes no comparison. Its only forward-looking statement is that a result below a cited threshold sends the reader to a GP, which is the opposite of a purchase prompt. The two figures are third-party ones quoted from the hub; no personal bloodwork appears anywhere. The single CTA is a soft in-post link to the canonical hub, which carries the test-selector routing onward, so nothing points at a kit or at the founding-member list. No em dashes, no bullet lists, no engagement bait.
